en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Confession (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Sahadhammika-vagga 74.
The Training Rule on Striking.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks, being angry and displeased, gave blows to the group-of-seventeen monks.
They wept.
The monks said this:
“Friends, why are you weeping?
“Friends, these monks of the group of six, being angry and displeased, are giving us blows.
Those monks who were of few desires … [as before] … complained, grumbled, and became indignant:
“How indeed can the group-of-six bhikkhus, being angry and displeased, give blows to other bhikkhus? … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, bhikkhus, that you, being angry and displeased, gave blows to other bhikkhus?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, being angry and displeased, give blows to the bhikkhus?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“Whosoever, being angry and displeased with a monk, should give him a blow, that is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
Whosoever, however...
Whoever such as this … [as before] … is a bhikkhu … [as before] …;
this is the kind of bhikkhu intended in this context.
"Of a bhikkhu" means of another bhikkhu.
"Angry and displeased" means...
Being dissatisfied, with a struck mind, and having become callous:

"He should give a blow" means that he gives a blow either with the body, or with something connected to the body, or with something released, even if it is only with a lotus leaf; there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one who is fully ordained perceives another as fully ordained, and being angry and displeased, gives them a blow, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one who is fully ordained is of doubtful perception, and being angry and displeased, gives them a blow, there is an offense of expiation.
If one who is fully ordained is perceived as not fully ordained, and being angry and displeased, gives them a blow, there is an offense of expiation.
If one, being angry and displeased, strikes one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one perceives as fully ordained someone who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one is in doubt regarding whether someone is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If [the person] is not ordained and one perceives them as not ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
There is no offense if,
while being harassed by someone, one strikes back with the intention of escaping.
"In the case of one who is insane,
and in the case of the first offender.
The fourth training rule on striking is concluded.
